parts.problem_md:
A student determines the density of the material used to make a metre rule.

Fig. 4.1 shows the metre rule (not drawn to scale).

![Diagram of a rectangular metre rule shown in 3D, with its small end labelled width w and thickness t for measurement.](assets/001-diagram-of-a-rectangular-metre-rule-shown-in-3d-.png)

**Fig. 4.1 (not to scale)**

(i) On Fig. 4.1, draw a double-headed arrow (↔) to show the length *L* of the metre rule.

[1]

(ii) Fig. 4.2 shows the actual size of the end of the metre rule.

![Rectangular bar shown in side view, labelled width w along the top and thickness t on the right with dashed dimension lines](assets/002-rectangular-bar-shown-in-side-view-labelled-widt.png)

**Fig. 4.2 (actual size)**

Use a ruler to measure width w and thickness t of the metre rule in Fig. 4.2.

Record each measurement to the nearest 0.1 cm.

[2]

(iii) The measurements in (a)(ii) are recorded to the nearest 0.1 cm.

State why it is not appropriate to record the measurements to the nearest 0.01 cm.

[1]

(iv) The length L of the metre rule is 100.0 cm.

Calculate the volume V of the metre rule.

Use your answers to (a)(ii) and the equation shown.

$V = L \times w \times t$

[1]
parts.solution_md:
(i)

![Diagram of a rectangular metre rule showing its length L, width w and thickness t, labelled along the edges of the three-dimensional block](assets/003-diagram-of-a-rectangular-metre-rule-showing-its-.png)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - dashed lines added to show both ends of the metre rule AND a double-headed arrow touching the dashed lines AND the arrow labelled L **[1 mark]**

(ii)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - w = 2.5 cm **[1 mark]**
> - t = 0.5 cm **[1 mark]**

(iii)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - the ruler only takes readings with a precision of 0.1 cm (has a smallest division of 0.1 cm) **[1 mark]**

(iv)

To calculate the volume of the metre rule:

- List the known quantities:

- Length, L = 100.0 cm
- Width, w = 2.5 cm
- Thickness, t = 0.5 cm

- Write down the equation:

$V = L \times w \times t$

- Substitute the known values:

$V = 100 . 0 \times 2 . 5 \times 0 . 5$

- Calculate the answer:

V = **125 cm^3^** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of 125 cm<sup>3</sup>
> 
> - Accept ecf (error carried forward) from part (a)(ii)

> **[exam-tip]**
> When drawing a dimension arrow on a diagram, always add dashed reference lines at both ends first, then draw the double-headed arrow between them and label it clearly — this makes it unambiguous exactly what length you're indicating.

parts.problem_md:
The student determines the mass *M* of the metre rule using a balancing method.

Procedure

The student:

**step 1** places a pivot directly under the 60.0 cm mark on the metre rule.

Fig. 4.3 shows the distance d = 60.0 cm.

![Diagram of a metre rule on a pivot at 50 cm, with a load at 60 cm, distance d = 60.0 cm from the 0 cm end, on a bench for moments experiment](assets/004-diagram-of-a-metre-rule-on-a-pivot-at-50-cm-with.png)

**Fig. 4.3 (not to scale)**

**step 2** places a load on the metre rule and adjusts the position of the load so that the rule balances

**step 3** records that the centre of the load is directly above the 67.1 cm mark on the metre rule.

(i) Calculate the distance $x_{1}$ from the centre of the load to the pivot.

[1]

**step 4** moves the pivot so that distance d = 70.0 cm

**step 5** adjusts the position of the load so that the metre rule balances

**step 6** records that the centre of the load is directly above the 84.2 cm mark on the metre rule

(ii) Calculate the distance $x_{2}$ from the centre of the load to the pivot.

[1]

(iii) Use the results for (b)(i) and (b)(ii) to calculate the mass M of the metre rule.

Use the equation shown.

`M = 5 \left(\right. x_{1} + x_{2} \left.\right)`

[1]
parts.solution_md:
(i)

To calculate the distance $x_{1}$ from the centre of the load to the pivot:

$x_{1} = 67 . 1 - 60 . 0$

x<sub>1</sub> = **7.1 cm** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct answer of 7.1 cm

(ii)

To calculate the distance $x_{2}$ from the centre of the load to the pivot:

$x_{2} = 84 . 2 - 70 . 0$

x<sub>2</sub> = **14.2 cm** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct answer of 14.2 cm

(iii)

To calculate the mass M of the metre rule:

`M = 5 \left(\right. x_{1} + x_{2} \left.\right) = 5 \left(\right. 7.1 + 14.2 \left.\right)`

M = **106.5 g** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct answer of 106.5 g
> 
> - Accept 106, 107, or 110

> **[exam-tip]**
> This method uses the principle of moments — measuring the load's balance position at two different pivot positions lets you calculate the rule's own mass without weighing it directly, by comparing how far the load must move each time.

parts.problem_md:
Use your answers to (a)(iv) and (b)(iii) to calculate the density ρ of the material used to make the metre rule.

Use the equation shown.

$ρ = \frac{M}{V}$

Give your answer to two significant figures.

Give the unit for your answer.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the density of the material:

$ρ = \frac{M}{V} = \frac{106.5}{125}$

**Final answer:** $ρ =$**0.852 g/cm^3^**

Rounding to two significant figures:

$ρ =$**0.85 g/cm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a calculation shown giving $0 . 852$
> 
> 1 mark for a correct answer of $0 . 85$, given to two significant figures
> 
> 1 mark for the correct unit, g/cm<sup>3</sup>
> 
> - Accept ecf from the candidate's own values in parts (a)(iv) and (b)(iii)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Density calculations often ask for a specific number of significant figures — always give your rounded final answer to exactly the number requested, and don't forget to state the unit, since it usually carries its own mark.

parts.problem_md:
You are going to determine the density of the material used to make a metre rule.

Fig. 4.1 shows the length L, width w and thickness t of a metre rule.

![Diagram of a metre rule showing its length L, with a side view indicating rectangular cross-section width w and small thickness t.](assets/006-diagram-of-a-metre-rule-showing-its-length-l-wit.png)

**Fig. 4.1 (not to scale)**

(i) Use the ruler to measure the width **w** and thickness **t** of your metre rule.

Record each measurement to the nearest $0 . 1 \text{cm}$.

[2]

(ii) The measurements in (a)(i) are recorded to the nearest $0 . 1 \text{cm}$.

State why it is not appropriate to record the measurements to the nearest $0 . 01 \text{cm}$.

[1]

(iii) The length L of the metre rule is $100 . 0 \text{cm}$.

Calculate the volume V of the metre rule.

Use your answers to (a)(i) and the equation shown.

$V = L \times w \times t$

[1]
parts.solution_md:
(i)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - w and t recorded AND w > t **[1 mark]**
> - both recorded to the nearest 0.1 cm **[1 mark]**

(ii)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - the ruler only takes readings with a precision of 0.1 cm (has a smallest division of 0.1 cm) **[1 mark]**

(iii)

Using the equation $V = L \times w \times t$ and your measured values of w and t from part (a)(i):

$V = L \times w \times t$

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - correct answer using the candidate's own measured values **[1 mark]**
> - must be consistent with the supervisor's results
> - accept 1 mm for 0.1 cm
> - ignore significant figures

> **[exam-tip]**
> In practical questions, your calculated answers must be consistent with your own measured values, not a fixed "correct" number — as long as your working correctly uses your recorded w and t, you'll gain the mark even if your raw measurements differ slightly from other students'.

parts.solution_md:

parts.problem_md:
A ball made of poly(ethene) has a density of 0.9 g/cm³.

Predict what happens to the ball when placed in a beaker of water and in a beaker of ethanol.

Use the data in Table 9.1 to explain your answer.

water: ..................

ethanol: ..................

explanation: ..................
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - water: floats AND ethanol: sinks **[1 mark]**
> - density of poly(ethene) is between the density of water (greater) and ethanol (lower) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> An object floats in a liquid if its density is lower than the liquid's density, and sinks if its density is higher. Compare the ball's density directly against each liquid's density from the table before deciding.

parts.problem_md:
A thin, flat piece of aluminium is used as a mirror.

(i) The piece of aluminium has a mass of 9.0 g.

Use information from Table 9.1 to calculate the volume of the piece of aluminium.

[2]

(ii) Fig. 9.2 shows a person’s eye looking at the reflection of an object placed in front of the aluminium mirror.

![Diagram showing a star-shaped object reflecting off a vertical mirror, with a ray path marked, towards an eye observing the reflection](assets/008-diagram-showing-a-star-shaped-object-reflecting-.png)

**Fig. 9.2**

On Fig. 9.2:

- draw the normal line and label the angle of incidence of the incident ray with the letter i.
- draw the reflected ray to show how the eye is able to see the reflected image of the object.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
(i)

To calculate the volume of the aluminium:

- List the known quantities:

- Mass, m = 9.0 g
- Density, $ρ = 2 . 7 \text{g} / \text{cm}^{3}$

- Write down the equation:

$ρ = \frac{m}{V}$

- Rearrange for volume:

$V = \frac{m}{ρ}$

- Substitute the known values:

$V = \frac{9.0}{2.7}$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the answer:

V = **3.3 cm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution into $V = \frac{m}{ρ}$ (accept formula in any form)
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of 3.3 cm<sup>3</sup>
> 
> - Accept 3 significant figures but no more

(ii)

![Ray diagram showing a star object and an eye viewing its reflection in a vertical plane mirror, with equal angle of incidence and reflection marked](assets/009-ray-diagram-showing-a-star-object-and-an-eye-vie.png)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - normal drawn correctly AND angle of incidence correctly shown **[1 mark]**
> - reflected ray to eye AND angle of reflection approximately equal to angle of incidence **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For ray diagrams, always draw the normal as a dashed line at right angles to the mirror at the point of reflection, then measure the angle of incidence and angle of reflection from this normal — not from the mirror surface itself.

parts.problem_md:
A solid block has a density of 1.1 g/cm<sup>3</sup>.

The block is lowered into three liquids, X, Y and Z, with different densities.

The densities of the liquids are:

liquid X: 1.0 g/cm<sup>3</sup>

liquid Y: 1.2 g/cm<sup>3</sup>

liquid Z: 1.3 g/cm<sup>3</sup>

In which of the liquids does the block float?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- An object floats when the liquid's density is greater than the object's density
- The block has a density of 1.1 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, so it floats only in liquids Y (1.2 g/cm<sup>3</sup>) and Z (1.3 g/cm<sup>3</sup>), which are both denser than the block
- It sinks in liquid X (1.0 g/cm<sup>3</sup>), which is less dense than the block

**A** is incorrect because the block also floats in liquid Z, since Z is denser than the block, not just Y

**C** is incorrect because the block sinks in liquid X, since X is less dense than the block

**D** is incorrect because the block floats in both Y and Z, but sinks in X, since X is less dense than the block

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: in liquids Y and Z only

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: in liquids X, Y and Z
